issues.legal_issue: A death certificate issued by respectable local persons is inadmissible to prove death when its makers were not legally required to maintain a record of deaths.
material_facts: The certificate was issued at the request of a family member by persons described as respectable residents of a place where the family had once lived.
There was no proof that the certificate’s makers had a legal duty to keep a death record.
The certificate was not shown to have come from the place where the death allegedly occurred.
issues.conclusion: The certificate did not satisfy section 35 of the Evidence Act and had no evidentiary value; the authorities erred in relying on it.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 35 of the Evidence Act, an entry in a public or official book, register, or record is relevant when it states a fact in issue or relevant fact and is made by a public servant in the discharge of official duty, or by another person performing a duty specially imposed by law. A certificate from private persons without such a legal duty does not meet that requirement. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.administrative_heir_claim_proceeding: The evidence is considered in an administrative proceeding to determine who should be recorded as an heir to a claim or property.
predicates.informal_death_certificate: A death certificate is issued by private local persons rather than as an official record made in the performance of an assigned legal duty.
predicates.issuer_legally_duty_bound_to_record_deat: The certificate’s issuer was legally required to maintain records of deaths.

issues.definition: When an heir-claim proceeding relies on an informal death certificate and its issuer had no legal duty to record deaths, the certificate is inadmissible and has no evidentiary value.

issues.legal_issue: An affected heir must be given an opportunity to be heard when a disputed death date determines the heir’s entitlement.
material_facts: The disputed date of death determined whether the deceased’s daughters could inherit under the applicable succession law.
The appellant challenged the exclusion of the daughters and sought to present evidence relevant to when the deceased had died.
The revisional authority dismissed the appellant’s challenge without giving her an opportunity to be heard.
The authority’s conclusion about the date of death relied on a certificate that was inadmissible.
issues.conclusion: The appellant should have been afforded an opportunity to be heard, and the decision made without that opportunity could not stand.
issues.legal_principle: The principles of natural justice require an opportunity to be heard where a disputed fact material to an affected person’s entitlement must be decided. Section 5(2) of the Displaced Persons (Claims) Supplementary Act, 1954, was invoked in relation to the opportunity to be heard. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.review_of_heir_substitution: An authority is reviewing a decision about which persons should be substituted or recorded as heirs.
predicates.death_date_determines_inheritance_rights: The date of death determines whether an affected person is entitled to inherit.
predicates.affected_heir_denied_opportunity_to_be_h: A person whose inheritance rights are affected was not given an opportunity to present their case before the decision was made.

issues.definition: In a review of heir substitution, when the death date determines inheritance rights, an affected heir denied a hearing must be given an opportunity to be heard.

issues.legal_issue: Death cannot be presumed from a person’s disappearance when the person has been unheard of for less than seven years by those who would naturally have heard from them if alive.
material_facts: The deceased disappeared and could not be traced after a police inquiry.
The question of death arose about two years after the disappearance.
The court considered whether a presumption of death arose from the disappearance.
issues.conclusion: No presumption of death arose because the deceased had been unheard of for only about two years.
issues.legal_principle: A presumption of death may arise when a person has not been heard of for seven years by those who would naturally have heard from that person if they had been alive. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.death_determination_proceeding: A proceeding requires a decision about whether or when a missing person died.
predicates.missing_person_unheard_of_by_natural_con: People who would naturally have heard from the missing person if that person were alive have heard nothing from them.
predicates.unheard_for_under_seven_years: The period during which the person has been unheard of is less than seven years.

issues.definition: In a proceeding to determine death, if a missing person has been unheard of by natural contacts for less than seven years, death cannot be presumed.

issues.legal_issue: When a Hindu coparcener dies after the Hindu Succession Act applies and leaves a qualifying female relative, the deceased’s interest in Mitakshara coparcenary property devolves by succession after determining that interest through a notional partition.
material_facts: The property was Mitakshara coparcenary property.
The deceased’s death was determined to have occurred after the Hindu Succession Act came into force.
He left a widow, three sons, and three daughters.
The court determined his interest by considering the share he would have received on a partition immediately before his death, and then determined succession to that interest among his heirs.
issues.conclusion: The deceased’s interest devolved by succession rather than survivorship. His widow, sons, and daughters shared that interest equally; the widow also received the share attributed to her on the notional partition.
issues.legal_principle: Section 6 of the Hindu Succession Act, including its proviso and Explanation I, provides that where a male Hindu dies with an interest in Mitakshara coparcenary property and leaves a female relative specified in Class I of the Schedule, his interest devolves by testamentary or intestate succession rather than survivorship. Explanation I determines that interest as the share that would have been allotted to him on a partition immediately before death. No earlier cases are relied on.

rule.if: inheritance_dispute and male_hindu_dies_after_succession_law_applies and property_is_mitakshara_coparcenary_property and surviving_class_one_female_relative and deceased_interest_determined_by_notional_partition

predicates.inheritance_dispute: A proceeding requires determination of the devolution of a deceased person’s property interest.
predicates.male_hindu_dies_after_succession_law_app: A male Hindu dies after the succession law applies to the succession in question.
predicates.property_is_mitakshara_coparcenary_prope: The property in which the deceased held an interest is Mitakshara coparcenary property.
predicates.surviving_class_one_female_relative: A female relative specified as a Class I heir survives the deceased.
predicates.deceased_interest_determined_by_notional: The deceased’s interest is determined by identifying the share that would have been allotted to him on a partition immediately before death.

issues.definition: In an inheritance dispute involving a male Hindu’s interest in Mitakshara coparcenary property, when he dies after the succession law applies, leaves a Class I female relative, and his interest is determined by notional partition, that interest devolves by succession to his heirs.
